## 1. Overview

Buses serve as a vital component of Singapore’s public transport network, connecting residential neighbourhoods, business hubs, and peripheral regions. To support the nation’s long-term mobility planning, this project conducts a comprehensive spatio-temporal analysis of commuter behaviour, moving beyond traditional mapping toward data-driven transport planning. By leveraging large-scale bus tap-on data, the study examines not only the intensity and distribution of passenger flows but also their spatial clustering and temporal dynamics.

The analysis is structured in three sections:

-   **Spatial Distribution Analysis**\
    Passenger trips are aggregated into a hexagonal Traffic Analysis Zone (TAZ) framework to build a clear spatial representation of mobility intensity during weekday morning, weekday evening, and weekend periods. This foundational layer visualises baseline travel flows and spatial distribution patterns across the island.

-   **Spatial Clustering**\
    To detect localised patterns of demand, the study applies Local Measures of Spatial Autocorrelation (LMSA) — including *Local Moran’s I*, *Geary’s C*, and *Getis-Ord Gi\** — to identify statistically significant hotspots, coldspots, and outlier areas of bus ridership.

-   **Temporal Trend Analysis**\
    To examine how these clusters evolve, Emerging Hot Spot Analysis (EHSA) integrates the Gi\* statistic with the Mann-Kendall trend test, classifying clusters as emerging, intensifying, diminishing, or sporadic over time. This captures the dynamic dimension of urban mobility.

### 1.1 Datasets

**Aspatial Data**

-   *Passenger Volume by Origin Destination Bus Stops* from [LTA DataMall](https://datamall.lta.gov.sg/content/datamall/en.html)

**Geospatial Data**

-   *Bus Stop Location* from LTA DataMall. It provides information about all the bus stops currently being serviced by buses, including the bus stop code (identifier) and location coordinates.

-   *Master Plan 2019 Subzone Boundary (No Sea)* from [Singapore’s open data portal](https://data.gov.sg/).

## 2. Data Preparation

### 2.1 Loading the R packages

The following R packages are used:

-   

    | R Package | Description |
    |------------------------------------|------------------------------------|
    | **sf** | A package that provides [**simple features access**](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simple_Features) for R. |
    | **spdep** | Creates spatial weights matrices and to test for and model spatial autocorrelation in geographical data, like Moran’s I and Geary’s C and Local Moran’s I and Getis-Ord G. |
    | **tidyverse** | Includes the core packages like ggplot2, dplyr, readr, purrr, tibble, lubridate, etc. |
    | **sfdep** | Builds on the great shoulders of **spdep** package for spatial dependence. sfdep creates an sf and tidyverse friendly interface to the package as well as introduces new functionality that is not present in spdep. |
    | **knitr** | Color maps designed to improve graph readability for readers with common forms of color blindness and/or color vision deficiency. |
    | **tmap** | geographical maps in which spatial data distributions are visualized. This package offers a flexible, layer-based, and easy to use approach to create thematic maps, such as choropleths and bubble maps. |
    | **rvest** | Provides the HTML parsing and extraction functions |
    | **patchwork** |  |

```{r}

pacman::p_load(tidyverse, sf, spdep, sfdep, knitr,tmap, rvest, patchwork)
```

### 2.2 Importing Data

#### 2.2.1 Bus Stop Location

We need to transform the data for EPSG:3414 Projected coordinate system for Singapore as bus Stop location data has crs = 9001,

```{r}

BusStop = st_read(dsn = "data/LTADataMall/",
                  layer = "BusStop") %>%
  st_transform(crs = 3414)
```

#### 2.2.2 Master Plan 2019 Subzone

```{r}
mpsz_sf <- st_read("data/geospatial/MasterPlan2019SubzoneBoundaryNoSeaKML.kml") %>%
  st_zm(drop = TRUE, what = "ZM") %>% st_transform(crs = 3414)
```

```{r}
plot(mpsz_sf)
```

```{r}
extract_kml_field <- function(html_text, field_name) {
  if (is.na(html_text) || html_text == "") return(NA_character_)
  
  page <- read_html(html_text)
  rows <- page %>% html_elements("tr")
  
  value <- rows %>%
    keep(~ html_text2(html_element(.x, "th")) == field_name) %>%
    html_element("td") %>%
    html_text2()
  
  if (length(value) == 0) NA_character_ else value
}
```

```{r}
mpsz_sf <- mpsz_sf %>%
  mutate(
    REGION_N = map_chr(Description, extract_kml_field, "REGION_N"),
    PLN_AREA_N = map_chr(Description, extract_kml_field, "PLN_AREA_N"),
    SUBZONE_N = map_chr(Description, extract_kml_field, "SUBZONE_N"),
    SUBZONE_C = map_chr(Description, extract_kml_field, "SUBZONE_C")
  ) %>%
  select(-Name, -Description) %>%
  relocate(geometry, .after = last_col())
```

```{r}
mpsz_cl <- mpsz_sf %>%
  filter(SUBZONE_N != "SOUTHERN GROUP",
         PLN_AREA_N != "WESTERN ISLANDS", 
         PLN_AREA_N != "NORTH-EASTERN ISLANDS")
```

```{r}
write_rds(mpsz_cl, 
          "data/rds/mpsz_cl.rds")
```

#### **2.2.2.1MRT Station**

Below we will import **Master Plan 2019 Subzone Boundary (No Sea).**

```{r}
mrt <- st_read("data/LTADataMall/LTAMRTStationExitKML.kml") %>%
  st_zm(drop = TRUE, what = "ZM") %>%
  st_transform(crs = 3414)
```

Below code is to write MRT station data into a rsd file, so we can directly call it without processing the data set again.

```{r}
#| eval: false
extract_kml_field <- function(html_text, field_name) {
  if (is.na(html_text) || html_text == "") return(NA_character_)
  
  page <- read_html(html_text)
  rows <- page %>% html_elements("tr")
  
  value <- rows %>%
    keep(~ html_text2(html_element(.x, "th")) == field_name) %>%
    html_element("td") %>%
    html_text2()
  
  if (length(value) == 0) NA_character_ else value
}

mrt_sf <- mrt %>%
  mutate(
    STATION = map_chr(Description, extract_kml_field, "STATION_NA"),
    EXIT_CODE = map_chr(Description, extract_kml_field, "EXIT_CODE"),
    INC_CRC = map_chr(Description, extract_kml_field, "INC_CRC"),
    FMEL_UPD_D = map_chr(Description, extract_kml_field, "FMEL_UPD_D")
  ) %>%
  
  # Just one exit for each station to avoid multiple points.
  filter(EXIT_CODE == "Exit A") %>%
  
  select(-Name, -Description) %>%
  relocate(geometry, .after = last_col())


write_rds(mrt_sf, "data/rds/mrt_sf.rds")
```

```{r}
mrt_sf <- read_rds("data//rds/mrt_sf.rds")
```

Plot the MRT station exits in a tmap.

```{r}
tmap_mode("view")
tm_shape(mpsz_cl) +

tm_shape(mrt_sf) +

#   popup = "STATION"

  )

```

#### 2.2.3 Origin Destination Bus Trips

```{r}
odbus <- read_csv("data/LTADataMall/origin_destination_bus_202508.csv")
```

##### 2.2.3.1 Visualise the Bus Stops

```{r}

#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 8

tm_shape(mpsz_cl) +
  tm_polygons() +
  tm_shape(BusStop) +
  tm_dots(size = 0.15, fill = "black", col = "grey") +
  tm_layout(bg.color = "lightblue",
            outer.margins = c(0.01, 0.01, 0.01, 0.01))
```

##### 2.2.3.2 Extract Bus Stops within Singapore

Some bus stops are outside the polygons because of JB border and they have to be excluded**.** One way to exclude them is to plot the mpsz layer on top of the BusStop layer.

```{r}
BusStop_in_SG <- st_join(
  BusStop, mpsz_cl,
  join = st_within,
  left = FALSE)
```

Plot the bus stop data again to check that the bus stops have been removed.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 8

tm_shape(mpsz_cl) +
  tm_polygons() +
  tm_shape(BusStop_in_SG) +
  tm_dots(size = 0.2, fill = "black", col = "grey") +
  tm_layout(main.title = "Bus Stops Within Singapore Boundaries",
            bg.color = "lightblue",
            outer.margins = c(0.01, 0.01, 0.01, 0.01))
```

##### 2.2.3.3 Deriving Analytical Hexagon

```{r}
hexagon <- st_make_grid(mpsz_cl,
                        cellsize = 750,
                        what = "polygon",
                        square = FALSE) %>%
  st_sf()
```

##### 2.2.3.4 Filtering hexagons with bus stops

To retain hexagons with bus stops. Use `st_intersects()` to return 2 values: True, False (0 or 1). The hexagon with a bus stop would be 1, and without a bus stop would return 0.

```{r}
hexagon$n_collisions =
  lengths(st_intersects(
    hexagon, BusStop_in_SG))

hexagon <- filter(hexagon, n_collisions > 0)
```

```{r}
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 8
tm_shape(mpsz_cl) +
  tm_polygons() +
  tm_shape(hexagon) +
  tm_fill(col = "grey20", fill = "orange", fill_alpha = 0.7) +
  tm_layout(bg.color = "lightblue",
            outer.margins = c(0.01, 0.01, 0.01, 0.01))
```

The hexagon map shows where bus stops are found across Singapore. Each colored hexagon marks an area with at least one bus stop, making it easy to see that most bus stops are located in built-up towns and along main roads. Many other parts of Singapore, especially less developed areas, don’t have direct bus service. This map gives us a clear base to group and analyze passenger numbers later. Since the hexagons don’t have names or numbers, we’ll give each one an ID so we can keep track of them more easily.

##### 2.2.3.5 Assigning ID to each hexagon

In order to know the trips occurred in each hexagon in certain time periods, we need to give each hexagon an ID.

```{r}
hexagon <- hexagon %>%
  select(,-n_collisions)

hexagon$HEX_ID <- sprintf(
  "H%04d", seq_len(nrow(hexagon))) %>%
  as.factor()

kable(head(hexagon))
```

#### 2.2.4 Preparing Trip Generation Data

We are only interested in ORIGIN_PT_CODE (trip origin).

##### 2.2.4.1 Cleaning the data

Only necessary columns are selected.

```{r}
trips <- odbus %>%
  select(c(ORIGIN_PT_CODE, DAY_TYPE, TIME_PER_HOUR, TOTAL_TRIPS)) %>%
  rename(BUS_STOP_N = ORIGIN_PT_CODE) %>%
  rename(HOUR_OF_DAY = TIME_PER_HOUR) %>%
  rename(TRIPS = TOTAL_TRIPS)
trips$BUS_STOP_N <- as.factor(trips$BUS_STOP_N)
kable(head(trips))
```

##### 2.2.4.2 Combining bus stop and hexagon layers

```{r}
bs_hex <-st_intersection(
  BusStop, hexagon) %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  select(c(BUS_STOP_N, HEX_ID))
kable(head(bs_hex))
```

##### 2.2.4.3 Adding Hex_ID into bus trips data

Use inner_join() to join trips and bus_hex

```{r}
trips <- inner_join(trips, bs_hex)
kable(head(trips))
```

```{r}
trips_sort <- trips %>%
  arrange(desc(TRIPS)) %>%
  mutate(HEX_ID = factor(HEX_ID, levels = unique(HEX_ID)))
```

```{r}
glimpse(trips_sort)
```

```{r}
ggplot(trips_sort,
  aes(x = HEX_ID, y = TRIPS, fill = HEX_ID)) +
  geom_col(fill = "blue") +
  labs(title = "Total Trips by HexID",
       x = "Hex ID", y = "Number of Trips") + 
  theme_minimal()
```

#### 2.2.5 Create Total Trips per Hexagon dataset

*Hexagon* spatial data and *trips* aspatial data will be joined for Local Measures of Spatial Association (LMSA) analysis. This is to allow us to view the spatial distribution of total bus trips.

##### 2.2.5.1 Aggregate Trip Data by Hexagon

Within *trips* dataset, we calculate the total TRIPS per hexagon ("HEX_ID").

```{r}
trips_agg <- trips %>%
  group_by(HEX_ID) %>%
  summarise(total_trips = sum(TRIPS, na.rm = TRUE),
            .groups = 'drop')

kable(head(trips_agg))
```

##### 2.2.5.2 Relational Join

Join *trips_agg* with *hexagon* on "HEX_ID".

```{r}
hexagon_trips <- hexagon %>%
  inner_join(trips_agg, by = "HEX_ID") %>%
  mutate(total_trips = replace_na(total_trips, 0))

kable(head(hexagon_trips))
```

## 3. **Spatial Distribution Analysis**

In section 2.3, we derived an analytical hexagon data of 375m to represent the traffic analysis zone (TAZ). We also processed

Time period filtering for 3 time intervals will be filtered to compute passenger trips generated by origin at hexagon level. This is also done with deriving an analytical hexagon data to represent the traffic analysis.

Weekday morning peak \>\>6am - 9am (Bus Tap Time)

Weekday afternoon peak \>\> 5pm - 8pm (Bus Tap Time)

Weekend/holiday \>\> 11am - 8pm (Bus Tap Time)

### 3.1 Peak Hour Trips by HexID

::: panel-tabset
## Weekday AM

Filter the Bus tap on the time between 6am to 9am as morning peak hours during weekdays.

```{r}
AM_weekday_sort <- trips_sort %>%
  filter(HOUR_OF_DAY %in% c(6, 7, 8, 9),
         DAY_TYPE == "WEEKDAY") %>%
  group_by(HEX_ID) %>%
  summarise(AM_TRIPS = sum(TRIPS)) %>%
  arrange(desc(AM_TRIPS))
```

```{r}

am_plot <- ggplot(AM_weekday_sort, 
       aes(x = reorder(HEX_ID, -AM_TRIPS), y = AM_TRIPS)) +
  geom_col(fill = "lightblue", alpha = 0.8) +
  labs(title = "Weekday Morning Peak Hour Passenger Trips (6-9 AM)",
       subtitle = paste("Total", format(sum(AM_weekday_sort$AM_TRIPS), big.mark = ","), 
                       "trips across", nrow(AM_weekday_sort), "traffic zones"),
       x = "Hexagon ID", 
       y = "Passenger Trips") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(panel.background = element_rect(fill = "#D0DDD0"),
        axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, size = 6),
        plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12),
        plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 9, color = "gray40")) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma)

# Display the plot
am_plot
```

## Weekday PM

Filter the Bus tap on the time between 5pm to 8pm as afternoon peak hours during weekdays.

```{r}
PM_weekday_sort <- trips_sort %>%
  filter(HOUR_OF_DAY %in% c(17, 18, 19, 20),
         DAY_TYPE == "WEEKDAY") %>%
  group_by(HEX_ID) %>%
  summarise(PM_TRIPS = sum(TRIPS)) %>%
  arrange(desc(PM_TRIPS))
```

```{r}
# PM Peak Visualization
pm_plot <- ggplot(PM_weekday_sort, 
       aes(x = reorder(HEX_ID, -PM_TRIPS), y = PM_TRIPS)) +
  geom_col(fill = "yellow", alpha = 0.8) +
  labs(title = "Weekday Afternoon Peak Hour Passenger Trips (5-8 PM)",
       subtitle = paste("Total", format(sum(PM_weekday_sort$PM_TRIPS), big.mark = ","), 
                       "trips across", nrow(PM_weekday_sort), "traffic zones"),
       x = "Hexagon ID", 
       y = "Passenger Trips") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(panel.background = element_rect(fill = "#D0DDD0"),
        axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, size = 6),
        plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12),
        plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 9, color = "gray40")) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma)

# Display the plot
pm_plot
```

## Weekend/PH

Filter the Bus tap on the time between 11am to 8pm as morning peak hours during weekend or holidays.

```{r}
weekend_sort <- trips_sort %>%
  filter(HOUR_OF_DAY %in% c(11:20),
         DAY_TYPE == "WEEKENDS/HOLIDAY") %>%
  group_by(HEX_ID) %>%
  summarise(WKD_TRIPS = sum(TRIPS)) %>%
  arrange(desc(WKD_TRIPS))
```

```{r}
# Weekend/Holiday Visualization
weekend_plot <- ggplot(weekend_sort,

max_trips <- max(c(max(weekend_sort$WKD_TRIPS),

# Weekend Pattern
weekend_plot <- ggplot(weekend_sort, 
       aes(x = reorder(HEX_ID, WKD_TRIPS), y = WKD_TRIPS)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#8B008B", alpha = 0.85, width = 0.8) +

       x = NULL,

    axis.title.x = element_text(size = 10, face = "bold"),

# COMBINE 
combined_plot <- am_plot + pm_plot + weekend_plot + 
  plot_layout(ncol = 3) +
  plot_annotation(
    title = "COMPARATIVE URBAN MOBILITY PATTERNS",
    subtitle = "Visualizing passenger trip volumes across different time periods in Singapore",
    caption = paste(
      "Data: 826 traffic analysis zones |",
      "Scale: 0 to", format(max_trips, big.mark = ","), "trips |",
      "Bars ordered by trip volume (high to low)"
    ),
    theme = theme(
      plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 18, hjust = 0.5, margin = margin(b = 10)),
      plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 14, hjust = 0.5, color = "gray40", margin = margin(b = 15)),
      plot.caption = element_text(size = 10, color = "gray50", hjust = 0.5, margin = margin(t = 10)),
      plot.background = element_rect(fill = "white", color = NA)
    )
  )

# Display the final plot
combined_plot
```

The chart shows the distribution of passenger trip volumes during three time periods in Singapore: weekday morning (6–9 AM), weekday evening (5–8 PM), and weekends/holidays (11 AM–8 PM). In all three periods, the curve rises steeply at the beginning and then levels off, indicating that a small number of zones account for a large share of total trips, while the majority of zones have relatively low passenger volumes. The evening period has the steepest curve, showing the highest concentration of trips in fewer zones, followed by the morning period. The weekend curve is slightly less steep, indicating a wider spread of passenger trips across zones compared to weekdays. Overall, trip volumes are not evenly distributed, with clear differences between weekday peaks and weekends.

## 4. Spatial Autocorrelation Analysis

### 4.1 Global Measures of Spatial Autocorrelation

```{r}
#| code-fold: true
# AM weekdays sorted by Hex ID
AM_weekday <- trips %>%
  filter(HOUR_OF_DAY %in% c(6, 7, 8, 9),
         DAY_TYPE == "WEEKDAY") %>%
  group_by(HEX_ID) %>%
  summarise(AM_TRIPS = sum(TRIPS)) %>%
  arrange(as.character(HEX_ID))

# PM weekdays sorted by Hex ID
PM_weekday <- trips %>%
  filter(HOUR_OF_DAY %in% c(17, 18, 19, 20),
         DAY_TYPE == "WEEKDAY") %>%
  group_by(HEX_ID) %>%
  summarise(PM_TRIPS = sum(TRIPS)) %>%
  arrange(as.character(HEX_ID))

# Weekend sorted by Hex ID
weekend <- trips %>%
  filter(HOUR_OF_DAY %in% c(11:20),
         DAY_TYPE == "WEEKENDS/HOLIDAY") %>%
  group_by(HEX_ID) %>%
  summarise(WKD_TRIPS = sum(TRIPS)) %>%
  arrange(as.character(HEX_ID))
```

```{r}
# Join all three datasets
hexagon_all <- hexagon %>%
  left_join(AM_weekday, by = "HEX_ID") %>%
  left_join(PM_weekday, by = "HEX_ID") %>%
  left_join(weekend, by = "HEX_ID") %>%
  mutate(across(c(AM_TRIPS, PM_TRIPS, WKD_TRIPS), 
                ~replace_na(., 0))) # Handle any NA values - we fill in zero for hexagons with no trips

# Check if join worked
names(hexagon_all)  
head(hexagon_all$PM_TRIPS)  
head(hexagon_all$AM_TRIPS)  
head(hexagon_all$WKD_TRIPS)  
```

This is for preparing the passenger trips data per hexagon area in `hexagon_all`.

#### **4.1.1 Compute (QUEEN) contiguity spatial weights**

This study examines whether passenger trips are evenly spread across all hexagons. Earlier charts already suggest that trips are unevenly distributed, and this section aims to confirm that using statistical evidence. Once unevenness is established, the next step is to determine whether there are specific clusters of high or low activity. If such clusters are found, the final step is to identify their exact locations.

```{r}
wm_q <- poly2nb(hexagon_all, queen = TRUE)
summary(wm_q)
```

The summary report above shows that there are 826 regions (hexagons) in the Singapore. The most connected area unit has 6 neighbours. 1 region has 0 neighbours (completely isolated).

The neighbour structure forms 6 separate connected subgraphs, meaning the entire study area is not fully connected. This can occur when some hexagons are isolated (e.g., near borders or water bodies).

```{r}
longitude <- map_dbl(hexagon_all$geometry, ~st_centroid(.x)[[1]])
```

```{r}
latitude <- map_dbl(hexagon_all$geometry, ~st_centroid(.x)[[2]])
```

```{r}
coords <- cbind(longitude, latitude)
head(coords)
```

```{r}
plot(hexagon_all$geometry, border="lightgrey")
plot(wm_q, coords, pch = 19, cex = 0.6, add = TRUE, col= "red")
```

#### **4.1.2 Row-standardised weights matrix**

Now we want to assign weights t =o each neighboring hexagon. In this study, each hexagon will be assigned equal weight (stylep = W).

```{r}
rswm_q <- nb2listw(wm_q,
                   style = "W", zero.policy = TRUE)
rswm_q
```

#### **4.1.3 Moran's I Test**

Moran's I statistics testing is being performed for the 3 different periods of time by using `moran.test()` from spdep package.

::: panel-tabset
## Weekday AM

**Moran's I Test**

```{r}
moran.test(hexagon_all$AM_TRIPS,
           listw = rswm_q,
           zero.policy = TRUE, na.action = na.omit)
```

**Insight**:

The Moran’s I statistic for weekday morning bus trips is 0.34, with an expected value near zero (–0.0012) and a p-value \< 2.2 × 10⁻¹⁶. This indicates that the observed value is much higher than expected under randomness. The large standard deviate (14.513) also supports this.

This means there is strong and statistically significant positive spatial autocorrelation in weekday morning passenger trips. In simpler terms, areas with high passenger volumes are located close to other areas with high volumes, and areas with low passenger volumes tend to cluster together as well.

This confirms that bus trip activity during morning peak hours is not randomly distributed across space but shows clear spatial clustering.

**Monte Carlo Moran's I** :simulation for 1,000 times.

```{r}
set.seed(1234)
bperm = moran.mc(hexagon_all$AM_TRIPS,
                 listw = rswm_q,
                 nsim = 999,
                 zero.policy = TRUE, na.action = na.omit)
bperm
```

The Monte Carlo simulation was run 1,000 times (999 simulations + 1 observed) to test the significance of the Moran’s I statistic more robustly. The observed Moran’s I is 0.34, which ranked 1,000 out of 1,000, meaning none of the simulated random distributions produced a value higher than the observed one.

The p-value of 0.001 indicates that the probability of observing such a strong Moran’s I by random chance is very low (0.1%). This provides strong statistical evidence that the spatial clustering pattern detected earlier is not due to random variation, but reflects a real spatial structure in the weekday morning bus trip data.

**Visualise Moran's I Test**

We plot the distribution of statistical values below.

```{r}
mean <- mean(bperm$res[1:999])
print(paste0("Mean of permutations: ", mean))

var <- var(bperm$res[1:999])
print(paste0("Variance: ", var))

summary(bperm$res[1:999])
```

```{r}
perm_data <- data.frame(moran_i = bperm$res)

ggplot(perm_data, aes(x = moran_i)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20, fill = "lightblue", color = "#DCDCDC") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, color = "blue", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.34, color = "red", linewidth = 0.5) +
  labs(x = "Simulated Moran's I (Weekday AM)", y = "Frequency") +
  theme(plot.background = element_rect("#D0DDD0"),
        panel.background = element_rect(fill = "#D0DDD0"))
```

The red line on the far right indicates the actual observed Moran’s I for weekday morning bus trips (≈ 0.34). This observed value lies far outside the bulk of the simulated distribution, showing that the observed spatial pattern is much stronger than what would occur by chance.

This visual evidence supports the earlier **Moran’s I test** and **Monte Carlo p-value**, confirming the presence of **significant positive spatial autocorrelation** in passenger trip volumes during the morning peak period.

## Weekday PM

**Moran's I Test**

```{r}
moran.test(hexagon_all$PM_TRIPS,
           listw = rswm_q,
           zero.policy = TRUE, na.action = na.omit)
```

**Insight**

For weekday evening trips, the Moran’s I statistic is 0.108, with an expected value close to zero (–0.0012). The p-value is 9.748 × 10⁻⁷, which is far below 0.05, indicating statistical significance. The standard deviate is 4.7586, confirming that the observed value is much higher than what would be expected by random chance.

Although the Moran’s I value for PM trips is **positive and significant**, it is **lower than the AM value (0.34)**, meaning that **spatial clustering is present but weaker** in the evening compared to the morning. Passenger trips during weekday evenings are still not randomly distributed, but the spatial pattern is **less tightly clustered**.

One likely reason for this weaker clustering is the greater variety in trip origins during the evening. Unlike the morning, when most trips are concentrated in residential areas heading toward key destinations, evening trips tend to start from a wider mix of locations — such as workplaces, schools, commercial districts, and shopping areas — resulting in a more scattered spatial pattern.

**Monte Carlo Moran's I**

```{r}
set.seed(1234)
bperm_pm = moran.mc(hexagon_all$PM_TRIPS,
                 listw = rswm_q,
                 nsim = 999,
                 zero.policy = TRUE, na.action = na.omit)
bperm_pm
```

The p-value of 0.001 provides strong evidence to reject the null hypothesis, confirming that **weekday PM passenger trips exhibit significant spatial clustering.** This Monte Carlo result supports and reinforces the analytical Moran’s I test, showing that the clustering pattern is unlikely to have occurred by random chance.

**Visualise Moran's I Test**

```{r}
mean_pm <- mean(bperm_pm$res[1:999])
print(paste0("Mean of permutations: ", mean))

var_pm <- var(bperm_pm$res[1:999])
print(paste0("Variance: ", var))

summary(bperm_pm$res[1:999])
```

```{r}
perm_data_pm <- data.frame(moran_i = bperm_pm$res)

ggplot(perm_data_pm, aes(x = moran_i)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20, fill = "yellow", color = "#DCDCDC") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, color = "blue", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.10792, color = "red", linewidth = 0.5) +
  labs(x = "Simulated Moran's I (Weekday PM)", y = "Frequency") +
  theme(plot.background = element_rect("#D0DDD0"),
        panel.background = element_rect(fill = "#D0DDD0"))
```

The red line on the far right represents the observed Moran’s I for weekday PM bus trips (≈ 0.108). Although lower than the AM peak value, this observed value still lies well outside the bulk of the simulated distribution, which is centered around zero (blue line). This indicates that the observed spatial pattern is stronger than what would be expected by chance.

This visual evidence **supports the PM Moran’s I test and Monte Carlo p-value (0.001)**, confirming that **significant positive spatial autocorrelation** exists during the evening peak period. However, the clustering effect is **weaker than in the morning**, reflecting a more dispersed spatial distribution of passenger trips.

## Weekend/Public holiday

**Moran's I Test**

```{r}
moran.test(hexagon_all$WKD_TRIPS,
           listw = rswm_q,
           zero.policy = TRUE, na.action = na.omit)
```

**Insight**

The Moran’s I statistic for weekend and public holiday trips is 0.235, with an expected value close to zero (–0.0012). The standard deviate of 10.078 and p-value \< 2.2 × 10⁻¹⁶ indicate that the observed value is far above what would be expected by random chance.

This provides **very strong statistical evidence** to reject the null hypothesis, confirming that **spatial clustering is present during weekends and public holidays**. The Moran’s I value is **lower than AM peak (0.34)** but **higher than PM peak (0.108)**, meaning the **weekend clustering is moderate**—more pronounced than in the evening but less concentrated than morning commutes.

This suggests that **weekend travel patterns are still spatially clustered**, likely reflecting popular leisure, shopping, and recreation areas, but with a more even distribution across the city compared to workday peaks.

**Monte Carlo Moran's I**

```{r}
set.seed(1234)
bperm_wkd = moran.mc(hexagon_all$WKD_TRIPS,
                 listw = rswm_q,
                 nsim = 999,
                 zero.policy = TRUE, na.action = na.omit)
bperm_wkd
```

The p-value of 0.001 provides strong evidence to reject the null hypothesis, confirming that **weekend and public holiday passenger trips exhibit significant spatial clustering**. This Monte Carlo result supports and reinforces the analytical Moran’s I test, indicating that the observed clustering pattern is highly unlikely to have occurred by random chance.

**Visualise Moran's I Test**

```{r}
mean_wkd <- mean(bperm_wkd$res[1:999])
print(paste0("Mean of permutations: ", mean))

var_wkd <- var(bperm_wkd$res[1:999])
print(paste0("Variance: ", var))

summary(bperm_wkd$res[1:999])
```

```{r}
perm_data_wkd <- data.frame(moran_i = bperm_wkd$res)

ggplot(perm_data_wkd, aes(x = moran_i)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20, fill = "#A376A2", color = "#DCDCDC") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, color = "blue", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.2349, color = "red", linewidth = 0.5) +
  labs(x = "Simulated Moran's I (Weekend)", y = "Frequency") +
  theme(plot.background = element_rect(fill = "#D0DDD0"),
        panel.background = element_rect(fill = "#D0DDD0"))
```

The histogram of simulated Moran’s I values for weekend/public holiday trips shows that most of the simulated values cluster around zero (blue line), representing the expected result under random spatial distribution. The observed Moran’s I value of 0.235 (red line) lies far to the right of the simulated distribution, clearly outside the main peak.
:::

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
| **Time Period** | **Moran's I** | **p-value** | **Clustering Strength** | **Pattern Description** |
| Weekday AM (6–9 AM) | 0.34 | \< 2.2e-16 | Strong | Concentrated commute flows from residential to key nodes |
| Weekday PM (5–8 PM) | 0.10792 | 0.001 | Weak | More dispersed origins, staggered travel times |
| Weekend/Public Holiday | 0.2349 | 0.001 | Moderate | Leisure-oriented flows, spread across multiple zones |

The highest clustering occurs during weekday morning peak, driven by concentrated commuting flows. The weakest clustering is during weekday evenings, when trip origins are more scattered and travel behaviour is less synchronized. Weekends and public holidays show a moderate level of clustering, indicating strong but more spatially distributed travel demand.

Clustering strength: **AM \> Weekend \> PM**.
